w: Two decades in the building, timed to open on the exact centenary of Uruguay's 1825 declaration of independence -- August 25, 1925. The seat of the General Assembly ever since, it was declared a National Historic Monument in 1975, monumental inside and out.
s: Uruguay's parliament, opened on independence's centenary
_facts: Meeting place of the General Assembly of Uruguay, seat of the legislative branch
Constructed 1904-1925; inaugurated 25 August 1925 for the centenary of independence
Declared a National Historic Monument in 1975

w: Named for the explorer who first sailed into these waters, Uruguay's grandest stage opened in 1856 and hosted the country's first homegrown opera, Giribaldi's La Parisina, in 1878. A six-year reconstruction added two Philippe Starck columns before it reopened in 2004.
s: Uruguay's grand opera house, opened in 1856
_facts: Uruguay's most important theatre, opened 1856, designed by Carlo Zucchi
Named after explorer Juan Diaz de Solis
First Uruguayan national opera, La Parisina, premiered here 14 September 1878
Major reconstruction 1998-2004 added two Philippe Starck-designed columns

w: At 157 metres, the tallest building in Uruguay, rising over the Bay of Montevideo as the headquarters of the state telecom company. Designed by Uruguayan-Canadian architect Carlos Ott and finished in 2002, it doubles as a monument to the painter Joaquin Torres Garcia.
s: Uruguay's tallest building, on the bay
_facts: 157-metre, 35-floor tower, headquarters of state telecom ANTEL
Tallest skyscraper in Uruguay
Designed by Carlos Ott, completed 2002
Also known as Torre Joaquin Torres Garcia

w: Montevideo's main Catholic church and seat of its archdiocese, standing watch over Constitution Square in the old town, with the colonial Cabildo directly across the plaza -- the historic heart of the city in one glance.
s: The city's main Catholic cathedral, on Constitution Square
_facts: Main Roman Catholic church of Montevideo, seat of the archdiocese
Located across Constitution Square from the Cabildo, in Ciudad Vieja

w: Named for the date Uruguay's first constitution was sworn in, this is the spine of Montevideo, running from Plaza Independencia to the Obelisk at Tres Cruces. It holds the city's best-preserved art deco architecture, including the Rinaldi, Diaz and Salvo palaces.
s: Montevideo's grand avenue of art deco palaces
_facts: Most important avenue in Montevideo, named for 18 July 1830 constitution
Runs from Plaza Independencia through Centro and Cordon to the Obelisk at Tres Cruces
Best-preserved art deco architecture in the city, e.g. Rinaldi, Diaz and Salvo palaces

w: Uruguay's seat of government for over a century, from 1880 until 1985, this neoclassical palace on Plaza Independencia still hosts state ceremonies today. A museum installed in 1999 fills its rooms with mementos from a century of presidents.
s: Uruguay's seat of government for over a century
_facts: Building on Plaza Independencia, completed 1873
Served as the country's seat of government 1880-1985
Neoclassical style; National Historic Monument since 1975
Museum established 1999, displaying presidency artifacts

w: Uruguay's oldest scientific institution, opened in 1838 and holding one of the oldest natural history collections anywhere. Its main exhibition hall occupies the former Miguelete Prison -- a building that swapped inmates for specimens over a century ago.
s: Uruguay's oldest scientific institution, in an old prison
_facts: Opened 1838, oldest scientific institution in Uruguay
One of the oldest natural history collections in the world
First permanent exhibition space at the former Miguelete Prison

w: The colonial government house of the Viceroyalty of the Rio de la Plata, standing on Constitution Square since Spanish rule. It now holds Montevideo's Historical Archive and a museum -- the closest thing the city has to a time capsule of its founding.
s: Colonial government house turned city museum
_facts: Used as the government house during colonial Viceroyalty of the Rio de la Plata
Now a museum and houses the Historical Archive of the city
Located on Constitution Square, Ciudad Vieja

w: A museum built entirely around memory -- of the Uruguayans who died or vanished under the dictatorship that ruled from 1973 to 1985. A somber, necessary counterpoint to the grander monuments elsewhere in the city.
s: A museum to the dictatorship's disappeared
_facts: MUME, museum dedicated to those who died or were disappeared during the Uruguayan dictatorship, 1973-1985

w: Montevideo's oldest public square, laid out in 1726 as the only open space inside the walled Fortress City of San Felipe and Santiago. Still the historic heart of town, ringed by the Cathedral and the Cabildo -- everything the old city built itself around.
s: Montevideo's oldest square, laid out in 1726
_facts: Also known as Plaza Matriz, oldest city square in Montevideo
Plaza mayor of the Fortress City of San Felipe and Santiago since 1726
Surrounded by the Metropolitan Cathedral and the Cabildo

w: Montevideo's city hall rose on the site of the old English Cemetery, designed by architect Mauricio Cravotto after a 1930s tender for a building meant for entirely different branches of government. Its esplanade is now where crowds gather to watch the national team on a giant screen.
s: City hall built on the old English Cemetery
_facts: Seat of Montevideo government on 18 de Julio Avenue, barrio Centro
Designed by architect Mauricio Cravotto
Built on the former English Cemetery property, originally meant for other branches of government
Esplanade is used to broadcast Uruguayan national team matches

w: A Roman Catholic parish church dedicated to St. Francis of Assisi, one of the quieter faith landmarks tucked into central Montevideo's streets.
s: A Catholic parish church in central Montevideo
_facts: Roman Catholic parish church in Montevideo
